cards.front: In the leak and push-back model of homeostasis, {{c1::leak}}, passive exchange with the surroundings, drags a regulated variable toward the outside value.
cards.back: Push-back from the effectors drags it the other way, toward the set point.
cards.quote: Leak, passive exchange with the surroundings, drags it toward the outside value.

cards.front: In a homeostatic loop, what are the effectors, and which way do they drag the regulated variable?
cards.back: The muscles, glands and organs that change the variable. Their push-back drags it toward the set point, the value it is held around.
cards.quote: Push-back from the effectors, the muscles, glands and organs that change the variable, drags it toward the set point

cards.front: In the leak and push-back model, how do the two pulls compare once a regulated variable has settled, and what then decides where it settles?
cards.back: They are equal, whatever the strengths: the effectors cancel exactly what leaks. The strengths decide where that balance falls.
cards.quote: Once the variable settles, the two pulls are equal, whatever the strengths; the effectors cancel exactly what leaks.

cards.front: In the leak and push-back model, inside shift = outside shift × leak strength ÷ ({{c1::leak strength + push-back strength}}).
cards.back: The stronger the push-back compared with the leak, the less the inside follows the outside.
cards.quote: inside shift = outside shift × leak strength ÷ (leak strength + push-back strength)

cards.front: How does the fraction of an outside change that reaches the inside separate a regulator from a conformer for one variable?
cards.back: A fraction near 0 makes the animal a regulator, holding the variable fairly steady; near 1, a conformer, letting it follow the outside within limits it can survive.
cards.why: The label applies to one named variable over a stated range of outside conditions.
cards.quote: A fraction near 0 makes the animal a regulator for that variable, holding it fairly steady; near 1, a conformer

cards.front: In the leak and push-back model, an animal's push-back is 9 times as strong as its leak. The outside temperature rises by 10 degrees C. How far does the inside shift after settling, and is the animal a regulator or a conformer for temperature here?
cards.back: Inside shift = 10 × 1 ÷ (1 + 9) = 1 degree C. A fraction of 0.1, near 0, so it regulates over this range.
cards.quote: The stronger the push-back compared with the leak, the less the inside follows the outside.

cards.front: In the leak and push-back model, a 10-degree outside change moves the inside by 5 degrees after settling. How strong is the push-back compared with the leak?
cards.back: Fraction = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 = leak ÷ (leak + push-back), so push-back equals leak.
cards.quote: The first film split a 10-degree outside change in half.

cards.front: What conditions does the simple leak and push-back model of homeostasis need in order to fit?
cards.back: A variable that exchanges passively with the outside, over one range of outside conditions, after settling, with the set point fixed and the effectors below their limit. Its numbers are a sketch.
cards.quote: It fits a variable that exchanges passively with the outside, over one range of outside conditions, after settling,

cards.front: {{c1::Homeostasis}} is the holding of a body variable within a range compatible with staying alive.
cards.back: Walter Cannon's word.
cards.quote: is the holding of a body variable within a range compatible with staying alive.
cards.section: The loop, part by part

cards.front: In the human core-temperature loop, which structure acts as the integrator?
cards.back: A region of the hypothalamus, which is nervous tissue.
cards.quote: In the first film's loop, the integrator is a region of the hypothalamus,
cards.section: The loop, part by part

cards.front: Why is a house thermostat with a furnace an imperfect analogy for the human temperature loop?
cards.back: The furnace can only heat. The body uses different effectors for each direction (sweating, shivering), turns one effector both ways (skin vessels widen in heat, narrow in cold), and uses behaviour as an effector too.
cards.quote: The body can use different effectors for each direction, such as sweating and shivering, and turn one effector both ways
cards.section: The loop, part by part

cards.front: A man sits in a room whose air is hotter than his skin. Of widened skin vessels and sweat, which can still carry heat out of him, and why?
cards.back: Sweat only. Widened vessels bring heat to the skin, but heat flows only from hot to cold, so hotter air cannot take it; evaporation of sweat is the only route left.
cards.quote: Widened vessels bring heat to the skin, but hotter air cannot take it; evaporation of sweat is the only route left.
cards.section: The loop, part by part

cards.front: Blagden's core temperature barely moved in rooms near or above the boiling point of water. Why do these trials show that the body pushed back, but not how hard?
cards.back: The trials lasted minutes, not hours, and a wet object also stays below the air temperature while it evaporates.
cards.quote: one more reason the brief trials show push-back but not its strength
cards.section: The loop, part by part

cards.front: A {{c1::tissue}} is a group of similar cells, with the material around them, that together do one kind of job.
cards.quote: A tissue is a group of similar cells, with the material around them, that together do one kind of job.
cards.section: Four tissues build the loop and the stomach wall

cards.front: Name the four animal tissue types and one job of each.
cards.back: Epithelial: sheets that cover surfaces, line cavities and control what crosses. Connective: cells in an extracellular matrix (bone, tendon, blood). Muscle: contracts to make movement or force. Nervous: neurons and glia that receive and send signals.
cards.quote: Most animals are built from four types, and the skin's temperature loop uses all four.
cards.section: Four tissues build the loop and the stomach wall

cards.front: Bone, tendon, fat and blood look nothing alike. Why do all of them count as connective tissue?
cards.back: Each is living cells spread through a nonliving extracellular matrix, a mesh of protein fibres and other material the cells secrete.
cards.quote: Connective tissue is living cells spread through a nonliving extracellular matrix, a mesh of protein fibres and other material the cells secrete.
cards.section: Four tissues build the loop and the stomach wall

cards.front: In the skin's temperature loop, give the tissue type and loop role of: a sweat gland, the smooth muscle around skin arteries, and temperature-sensitive nerve endings.
cards.back: Sweat gland: epithelium, effector. Smooth muscle: muscle tissue, effector (narrows arteries to keep heat in). Nerve endings: nervous tissue, sensors. The hypothalamic integrator is nervous tissue too.
cards.quote: Temperature-sensitive nerve endings in the skin, and nerve cells in the brain, are the loop's sensors; the hypothalamic integrator is nervous tissue too.
cards.section: Four tissues build the loop and the stomach wall

cards.front: An {{c1::organ system}} is a set of organs that share a larger job, such as the digestive system that includes the stomach.
cards.back: An organ is a structure built from several tissues that work together.
cards.quote: An organ system is a set of organs that share a larger job
cards.section: Four tissues build the loop and the stomach wall

cards.front: A disease destroys the epithelial lining of a stomach wall but leaves its connective tissue and muscle intact. Which job is lost, and which continues?
cards.back: The lining that controls what crosses into the wall is lost. The muscle can still squeeze and churn the contents, and connective tissue still holds the layers together.
cards.why: Each tissue does one kind of job; losing one tissue removes that job, not the others.
cards.quote: Epithelial tissue is a sheet of closely joined cells that covers the body's surfaces and lines its cavities and tubes.
cards.section: Four tissues build the loop and the stomach wall

cards.front: As a leaf's water status falls, its stomata close. Label the regulated variable and effector, and say whether this is negative or positive feedback.
cards.back: Regulated variable: leaf water status. Effector: the stomata. Negative feedback: closing slows water loss, opposing the fall.
cards.quote: as a leaf's water status falls, its stomata, the pores in its surface, close, which slows water loss.
cards.section: Four tissues build the loop and the stomach wall

cards.front: Shivering raises body temperature. Why is it still negative feedback?
cards.back: "Negative" names the direction of the push relative to the deviation, not the direction of the change. Shivering opposes a fall in temperature.
cards.quote: names the direction of the push, not of the change
cards.section: Negative and positive feedback, and set points that move

cards.front: What is positive feedback?
cards.back: A response that pushes the variable further from where it started, amplifying the change.
cards.quote: In positive feedback, the response pushes the variable further from where it started.
cards.section: Negative and positive feedback, and set points that move

cards.front: Trace the positive-feedback loop in the textbook model of human labour, and say what ends it.
cards.back: Cervical stretch promotes oxytocin release, which strengthens uterine contractions, which stretch the cervix further. Something outside the loop, the birth of the baby, ends it.
cards.quote: stretch of the cervix promotes release of the hormone oxytocin, which strengthens contractions of the uterus, which stretches the cervix further
cards.section: Negative and positive feedback, and set points that move

cards.front: In the model with the push flipped away from the set point, inside shift = outside shift × leak ÷ (leak − push). The push is half as strong as the leak and the outside shifts by 4 units. What is the inside shift? What if the push were twice the leak?
cards.back: 4 × 1 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = 8 units: doubled, but it still settles. With push twice the leak there is no stable balance, and any change keeps growing.
cards.quote: Positive feedback runs away only when the push is stronger than the leak.
cards.section: Negative and positive feedback, and set points that move

cards.front: Mice that lack oxytocin entirely gave birth without obvious problems but could not let down milk. What does this show about the oxytocin labour loop?
cards.back: The loop is a model of human labour; as drawn, it does not carry over to every mammal.
cards.quote: mice that lack oxytocin entirely gave birth without obvious problems, though they could not let down milk
cards.section: Negative and positive feedback, and set points that move

cards.front: At the start of a fever, a person's core temperature is still at its usual value. What does she feel and do, and why?
cards.back: She feels cold and shivers. The set point has risen, so her normal temperature now reads as below it, and negative feedback pushes temperature up toward the new set point.
cards.quote: In a fever the set point for core temperature rises, so a person at normal temperature feels cold and shivers.
cards.section: Negative and positive feedback, and set points that move

cards.front: In {{c1::feedforward}} control, a signal that predicts a disturbance triggers the response before the variable changes.
cards.quote: In feedforward control, a signal that predicts a disturbance triggers the response before the variable changes
cards.section: Negative and positive feedback, and set points that move

cards.front: What is the difference between an endotherm and an ectotherm?
cards.back: An endotherm warms its body mainly with heat from its own metabolism (mammals, birds). An ectotherm gets its body heat mainly from its surroundings.
cards.quote: An endotherm warms its body mainly with heat from its own metabolism
cards.section: Regulators and conformers, and the price of constancy

cards.front: A desert lizard gets most of its body heat from the sun and shuttles between sun and shade to keep its body temperature fairly steady. Classify it as endotherm or ectotherm, and as regulator or conformer.
cards.back: An ectotherm that regulates, with behaviour as its effector. The two pairs of terms answer different questions.
cards.why: Endotherm and ectotherm say where the heat comes from; regulator and conformer say how far the body follows the outside.
cards.quote: Endotherm and ectotherm say where the heat comes from; regulator and conformer say how far the body follows the outside.
cards.section: Regulators and conformers, and the price of constancy

cards.front: Two marine invertebrates are moved from full-strength into half-strength seawater. After several days, animal A's blood osmolality is close to the new water's; animal B's stays well above it. Name each, and estimate each one's fraction in the leak and push-back model.
cards.back: A is an osmoconformer, fraction near 1; B is an osmoregulator over this range, fraction nearer 0. Like the mussel and the shore crab.
cards.why: The fraction is how much of the outside change reaches the inside; near 0 means regulator, near 1 conformer.
cards.quote: For blood salt, where the variable is osmolality, the concentration of dissolved particles in a fluid, the terms are osmoregulator and osmoconformer
cards.section: Regulators and conformers, and the price of constancy

cards.front: Why does holding core temperature steady in a cool room cost an endotherm energy?
cards.back: Staying near the set point requires the effectors to cancel what leaks; in a cool room that means making as much heat as leaks out.
cards.quote: in a cool room, that means making as much heat as leaks out.
cards.section: Regulators and conformers, and the price of constancy

cards.front: A mouse holds its core near 37 degrees C in rooms at 30, 22 and 15 degrees C. Assuming its effectors stay below their limit, rank the rooms by how hard its effectors work, and explain.
cards.back: 15 > 22 > 30 degrees C. A colder room means a bigger gap between body and air, so heat leaks out faster and more heat production must make it up.
cards.why: Leak is a fixed strength times the gap to the outside.
cards.quote: A colder room means a bigger gap between body and air, so heat leaks out faster
cards.section: Regulators and conformers, and the price of constancy

cards.front: How did one 2022 study measure mouse energy expenditure at 22 versus 30 degrees C, and what did it find?
cards.back: Indirect calorimetry, from oxygen used and carbon dioxide produced. Expenditure was about 30% higher at 22 degrees C.
cards.quote: found it about 30% higher at 22 degrees C than at 30 degrees C.
cards.section: Regulators and conformers, and the price of constancy

cards.front: Assume a mouse spends 20 kJ per day at 30 degrees C and that expenditure at 22 degrees C is exactly 1.30 times as much. Find its daily expenditure at 22 degrees C, the extra daily cost, and the extra cost over 30 days.
cards.back: 20 × 1.30 = 26 kJ per day. Extra: 26 − 20 = 6 kJ per day. Over 30 days: 6 × 30 = 180 kJ.
cards.quote: The 30% is measured; the baseline is invented for arithmetic.
cards.section: Regulators and conformers, and the price of constancy

cards.front: Expenditure at 22 degrees C is exactly 1.30 times that at 30 degrees C. A mouse moves from 22 to 30 degrees C. By what percentage does its expenditure fall, and why is it not 30%?
cards.back: Fall = 0.30 ÷ 1.30 = 0.231, about 23.1%. A percentage change uses the starting value as its base, and the start is now the larger value.
cards.quote: A percentage change uses the starting value as its base
cards.section: Regulators and conformers, and the price of constancy

cards.front: Suppose a cooler room raised expenditure by 50%. Moving back to the warmer room, by what percentage would expenditure fall? State the general rule.
cards.back: 0.50 ÷ 1.50 = 0.333, about 33%. A rise and the reverse fall differ because each uses its own starting value as the base; the fall's base is the larger value.
cards.quote: because the base is now the larger value.
cards.section: Regulators and conformers, and the price of constancy

cards.front: What is a mouse's thermoneutral point, and why does that make 30 degrees C an imperfect zero-cost baseline?
cards.back: The air temperature at which it spends no extra energy to hold body temperature. It is not one number: near 29 degrees C in the light phase and 33 degrees C in the dark.
cards.quote: found thermoneutral points near 29 degrees C in the light phase and 33 degrees C in the dark
cards.section: The mouse energy study: scope and mouse thermoneutral points

cards.front: A thirsty mouse stops drinking before water is absorbed. Design a stomach-infusion comparison that tells whether stomach stretch or gut sensing of dilution silences thirst neurons.
cards.back: Infuse water in one group and an equal volume of hypertonic salt solution in another. If stretch alone mattered, both would silence the neurons; if the gut senses dilution, only water should.
cards.quote: Give one group water and another an equal volume of concentrated (hypertonic) salt solution.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In mice, water in the stomach silenced thirst-promoting neurons within about 105 to 107 seconds, before any detectable change in blood osmolality, while hypertonic saline activated them. What kind of control does this reveal?
cards.back: A feedforward signal from the gut, acting on top of negative feedback from the blood, because the neurons responded before the blood changed.
cards.why: Limit: "no detectable change" depends on how sensitive the blood assay is.
cards.quote: Neural activity falling before blood changes means a feedforward signal on top of negative feedback from the blood.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How would you test whether the vagus nerves carry the gut's water signal to thirst circuits, and what result would support it?
cards.back: Compare vagotomy (cutting the vagus nerves below the diaphragm) with a sham operation (nerves exposed, not cut). If water's suppression of drinking weakens only after vagotomy, the vagus carries part of the signal.
cards.quote: If the effect weakens only after vagotomy, the vagus carries part of the signal.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a hot room with steamy, saturated air, sweat cannot evaporate. Using the leak and push-back model, predict what happens to core temperature and which condition of the model fails.
cards.back: Push-back reaches its limit, so the inside begins to follow the outside and core temperature rises. The model's condition that the effectors stay below their limit fails.
cards.why: Sweat evaporation is the only route for heat out when air is hotter than skin.
cards.quote: In humid air sweat evaporates slowly, push-back reaches its limit, and the inside begins to follow the outside.
cards.section: The loop, part by part

cards.front: Is normal human core temperature exactly 37 degrees C?
cards.back: No. The set point is a reference around which the normal range fluctuates, near, not exactly, 37 degrees C; normal also follows a daily rhythm and depends on where it is measured.
cards.quote: the set point is a reference around which the normal range fluctuates, near, not exactly, 37 degrees C for core temperature
cards.section: The loop, part by part
